strengths: Originality/significance: Applying a last-layer Laplace approximation to obtain instance-conditioned reference-score distributions from one trained reference model is a novel and potentially useful direction for reducing the cost of membership inference audits.
Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover five tabular and image datasets and compare against Attack-P, Attack-R, LiRA, QMIA, and RMIA under several reference-model budgets.
The paper includes informative studies of posterior sample count, Hessian approximation, predictive approximation, prior tuning, architecture mismatch, and out-of-distribution nonmembers.
The main empirical results are promising: BMIA reports substantially better low-FPR TPR than the tested baselines while requiring only one reference model.
The paper states its main computational limitation and generally presents the proposed pipeline clearly.
weaknesses: Soundness: Algorithm 1's one-sample t-test is not a valid test of whether the single target score belongs to the nonmember predictive distribution. All differences d_i share the same target score, while posterior Monte Carlo draws are treated as independent observations and the standard error is divided by sqrt(N). Consequently, increasing an arbitrary computational sample count can make any nonzero score difference increasingly significant. The resulting p-value does not have the claimed nominal FPR interpretation. A predictive quantile or posterior-predictive check would address a different and more appropriate question.

Soundness: Proposition 4.2, which claims that conditional attacks are always at least as powerful as marginal attacks, is not established. Equation (30) factorizes an expectation of a ratio into products without justified independence. Moreover, in the stipulated low-TPR regime the relevant numerator is negative, so multiplying Jensen and variance inequalities reverses directions used in Equations (32)-(33). The proposition is generally too strong without additional assumptions.

The probabilistic derivation contains basic sign and scaling errors. With L minimized as a negative log-posterior, log p(w|D) should involve -L, and the covariance is based on the inverse positive Hessian of L, not (-∇²L)^-1. The Gaussian-prior curvature should scale as γ^-2 rather than γ². Although the implementation uses an existing library, these errors undermine the methodological account.

The central uncertainty motivation is overstated. Sampling last-layer weights primarily represents approximate parameter uncertainty; sampling logits and computing hinge scores does not by itself incorporate aleatoric label uncertainty. Conversely, quantile regression estimates conditional outcome quantiles, so the claim that it categorically captures only aleatoric uncertainty does not directly establish that BMIA estimates the required across-training-set score distribution more accurately.

The empirical evidence does not repair the inferential problems. It is unclear whether Table 1 uses Algorithm 1's nominal p-value threshold or retrospectively sweeps/calibrates scores to achieve each reported FPR. These procedures have different meanings, and the paper does not demonstrate FPR calibration.

Reliability and reproducibility are inadequate for low-FPR claims: no repeated trials, confidence intervals, random seeds, exact evaluation-set counts, target/reference accuracies, hardware specification, or complete implementation link are provided. At 0.1% FPR, some dataset splits may yield very few false positives, making uncertainty reporting essential.

Presentation contains material numerical inconsistencies. The abstract attributes a 37.5% TPR at 1% FPR and a 64% improvement to CIFAR-10, whereas Table 1 reports 8.87% for CIFAR-10 and 35.75% for CIFAR-100; even the latter is about a 54% relative improvement over LiRA's 23.20%. Section 5.2 also describes 0.01% and 0.1% FPR while Table 1 reports 0.1% and 1%. Several displayed formulas use inconsistent signs, and page 15 has a malformed header/footer.

The efficiency comparison reports reference-model training time but does not provide a complete end-to-end accounting of Laplace fitting, Hessian construction/storage, sampling, hyperparameter optimization, and baseline tuning under matched hardware. Thus, the precise magnitude of the claimed savings is difficult to verify.

The limitations and impact discussions are insufficient. The limitations omit the Laplace/last-layer approximation's calibration assumptions and possible failure under training-procedure or distribution mismatch. The impact statement dismisses specific consequences despite membership inference being dual-use and despite experiments involving health and purchase datasets; authorized auditing, misuse risks, and data-handling considerations should be discussed.

Overall, the idea has merit, but the invalid statistical test and unsupported central theorem are fundamental deficiencies. Substantial methodological correction and a statistically rigorous reevaluation are required before the reported gains can support acceptance.

strengths: The core idea—using a last-layer Laplace approximation to obtain instance-dependent reference-score distributions from one reference model—is practically motivated and appears novel as an application to membership inference.

The empirical scope is broad, covering CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, Texas-100, and Purchase-100, several target/reference architectures, an OOD setting, and ablations of posterior sample count, curvature approximation, prior tuning, and predictive approximation.
The reported attack performance is potentially significant: BMIA often exceeds eight-reference-model baselines while requiring only one reference-model training run.
The paper is generally organized clearly, and its limitations section candidly notes that one-reference-model BMIA may lose to more expensive approaches when computation is abundant.
weaknesses: Soundness: Algorithm 1's one-sample t-test is not a calibrated membership test. Under the non-member hypothesis, the observed target score s0 and sampled reference scores may share a marginal distribution, but conditional on s0, E[s0-si] is generally not zero. Unconditionally, all di share s0 and are correlated, whereas the reported standard error treats them as independent. Indeed, increasing N drives the stated standard error toward zero while omitting uncertainty in s0, so the nominal p-value need not control FPR at alpha. The experiments report ROC operating points but do not test whether the algorithmic rule p<alpha actually achieves its claimed FPR.

Soundness: Proposition 4.2 is not established. Equation (30) improperly factorizes an expectation involving muS(z), muD(z), sigmaD(z), and 1/sigmaS(z); these quantities need not be independent. Subsequent Jensen and variance-decomposition inequalities also depend on unproven sign and pointwise-domain conditions. Consequently, the claimed general dominance of conditional over marginal attacks is unsupported and is likely false without substantially stronger assumptions.

The central modeling bridge is insufficiently justified: posterior samples around one model trained on one fixed reference dataset are treated as surrogates for the distribution induced by retraining models on random datasets. These are different distributions, and no theorem or calibration experiment establishes that last-layer Laplace uncertainty estimates the required Q|z. Relatedly, a Gaussian logit vector does not imply a Gaussian hinge score because the score contains a maximum over competing logits.

The Bayesian formulation contains basic sign inconsistencies: L is minimized in Equation (11), but is then equated with log p(w|D), followed by a negative Hessian and a negative-definite expression in Equation (12). This obscures what covariance is actually approximated and weakens the methodological presentation.

The evaluation lacks repeated trials, confidence intervals, significance tests, and explicit evaluation-set counts. This is especially problematic for TPR at 0.1% FPR, where estimates can depend on very few false positives. Target/reference accuracies and calibration diagnostics are also absent, and the text inconsistently describes Table 1 as evaluating 0.01% and 0.1% FPR although the table uses 0.1% and 1%.

The efficiency comparison is not end-to-end: Table 1 counts reference or quantile-model training, while Laplace fitting and attack inference are excluded or only qualitatively called minimal. Hardware is unspecified, baseline tuning details are incomplete, and the default posterior sample count is unclear, limiting both fairness and reproducibility. No artifact or code-release statement is provided beyond citing the generic Laplace library.

Originality and significance are promising but presently constrained by the unsupported identification of Bayesian posterior uncertainty with retraining variability and by the invalid statistical test; strong empirical numbers cannot compensate for these central issues.

The limitations and ethics treatment is inadequate. The stated limitation covers only computational regimes, not calibration failure, approximation error, distribution shift, or attacker-knowledge assumptions. The impact statement dismisses specific consequences despite membership inference being a dual-use privacy attack, and it offers no discussion of misuse or safeguards, including for the sensitive hospital-record benchmark.

strengths: Originality/significance: BMIA is a useful and relatively novel combination of last-layer Laplace approximation with conditional membership inference. Replacing an ensemble of reference models with posterior samples from one model could materially reduce the cost of privacy auditing.

Empirical scope: Table 1 covers five datasets spanning tabular and image classification, several target architectures, three strong conditional-attack families (LiRA, RMIA, and Attack-R), QMIA, and a marginal baseline. BMIA reports especially strong low-FPR results, including 13.11% TPR at 0.1% FPR on CIFAR-100 and competitive ImageNet performance with one reference model.

The evaluation includes relevant diagnostic experiments: posterior sample count and inference time (Figure 3), mismatched target/reference architectures (Figure 4), curvature approximations (Figure 5), prior tuning (Figure 6), predictive-distribution approximations (Figure 7), and shifted CINIC-10 non-members (Table 2).

Presentation is generally well organized, and the main motivation, threat model, algorithm, and efficiency-performance tradeoff are easy to identify. The rendered paper is visually clean, with legible tables and figures.

The limitations section honestly acknowledges that a single local Laplace approximation may lose to multi-model approaches under a larger compute budget and suggests mixture approximations as future work.
weaknesses: Soundness: Algorithm 1's one-sample t-test is not a calibrated membership test. Every difference d_i=s_0-s_i shares the single target score s_0; increasing the number of posterior samples therefore drives the standard error toward zero even though uncertainty in the target draw does not vanish. Under identical symmetric target and reference score distributions, the stated test would asymptotically reject for roughly every target score above the reference mean, rather than at the nominal alpha. A posterior-predictive tail probability or properly derived two-sample/predictive test is needed. This directly undermines the claimed interpretation of its p-values and conditional thresholds, even if the resulting standardized statistic can still rank examples well in an empirically calibrated ROC.

The main theoretical claim is unsupported. Proposition 4.2 asserts that conditional attacks always have at least the power of marginal attacks, but its proof moves from the expectation of a ratio to a product of expectations in Equation 30 without justified independence, and subsequent inequalities depend on signs that need not hold. The proposition on page 5 also uses the opposite sign for the Phi^{-1}(alpha) term from Equation 28 and Proposition 4.1. Consequently, the claimed guarantee does not follow from the stated assumptions.

The Bayesian justification is incomplete: posterior weight samples conditioned on one fixed reference dataset are not shown to approximate the distribution of scores induced by retraining models on independently sampled datasets, which is what LiRA-style conditional reference distributions represent. Moreover, with a fixed label and deterministic logits, last-layer weight sampling primarily represents parameter uncertainty; the repeated claim that the procedure directly captures both epistemic and aleatoric score uncertainty needs a precise likelihood-level derivation or ablation.

There are additional mathematical inconsistencies. The manuscript equates log p(w|D) with a loss L that Equation 11 minimizes, uses a questionable prior-curvature coefficient -gamma^2 I in Equation 12 where the stated Gaussian prior implies -1/gamma^2 I, and alternates between full-weight/full-covariance descriptions and the last-layer KFAC method actually evaluated. These are not merely stylistic because they obscure the exact implemented posterior.

Reproducibility/evidential strength is insufficient for the unusually large gains: the paper does not report random seeds, numbers of independent target/reference-model trials, confidence intervals, evaluation-set counts, or the default posterior sample count. At 0.1% FPR, finite-sample variability is particularly important. No implementation artifact is identified beyond the generic Laplace library.

The efficiency comparison reports only training time in Table 1, omitting Laplace fitting, curvature construction, hyperparameter optimization, sampling, and attack inference from the principal cost measure. Hardware and timing methodology are also unspecified. The paper should compare total wall-clock/GPU cost and memory under matched implementations.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: Section 5.2 says Table 1 evaluates 0.01% and 0.1% FPR although the table reports 0.1% and 1%; the introduction's CIFAR-10 example appears inconsistent with Table 1; and frequent grammatical and notation errors reduce precision.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The discussion does not address failure of local/last-layer Laplace approximations, calibration of the nominal FPR, or the absence of repeated-run uncertainty. The Impact Statement says no consequences need highlighting, despite membership inference being a dual-use privacy attack and the evaluation including sensitive health-record-derived data; misuse risks, safeguards, and dataset governance deserve explicit treatment.

strengths: [Originality/significance] BMIA is a creative post-hoc use of last-layer Laplace approximation for reducing the cost of conditional membership inference; the single- and multi-reference formulations address a practically important bottleneck.

[Empirical scope] The evaluation spans image, tabular, and text datasets, multiple architectures, architecture/distribution mismatch, alternative Bayesian approximations, Hessian factorizations, and sample-count ablations.

[Empirical results] The reported gains are often substantial: for example, single-reference BMIA reaches 35.75% TPR at 1% FPR on CIFAR-100 versus 23.20% for eight-reference LiRA, with much lower reported reference-training cost.

[Presentation] The motivation, algorithms, variance decomposition, and computational scaling of last-layer KFAC/diagonal Laplace approximations are generally explained clearly. weaknesses: [Soundness—decisive] Algorithm 1's nominal t-test is not justified for the actual single-reference setting. Conditional on one reference dataset, posterior samples share a dataset-specific center, whereas the target score comes from a separately trained MAP model. They are therefore not i.i.d. draws from one Gaussian. Indeed, Proposition 3.1 says target-versus-reference variance contains an inter-model term, but Algorithm 1 estimates only posterior within-model variance. Consequently, its claimed p-values and FPR control do not follow from the presented analysis.

[Soundness—decisive] Theorem 3.2 is not proved. Its argument varies M while treating the random sample mean, estimated variance, degrees of freedom, and t critical value as fixed; all change with M. A reduced variance expression alone does not establish strictly increasing power, especially under the model mismatch above. The statement also claims all alpha in (0,1), while the proof explicitly needs alpha<0.5 and positive intra-model variance.

[Soundness] Proposition B.2 contains invalid steps. Equation (32) factors an expectation of a ratio without independence or constancy assumptions, and subsequent Jensen/variance inequalities ignore the sign of the numerator; under the stated TPR(z)<0.5 condition that sign is negative, reversing relevant inequalities. Thus the broad claim that conditional attacks provably dominate marginal attacks is unsupported.

[Methodological mismatch] Proposition 3.1 assigns the target MAP score both inter- and posterior intra-model variance, although the target model is not sampled from its posterior. Appendix A.3 establishes only an asymptotic analogy for Gaussian linear regression and explicitly notes a dataset-dependent center gap; it does not validate the neural-network test used here. Algorithm 2 additionally does not explain how negative estimates of inter-model variance in Equation (40) are handled.

[Evaluation/reproducibility] Results at 0.1% FPR are reported without confidence intervals or the effective number of negative examples, making tail estimates potentially noisy. Table 9 varies reference models only on CIFAR-10; uncertainty across target-model seeds and datasets is absent. It is also unclear whether tabulated TPRs use the claimed nominal p<alpha rule or empirically selected ROC thresholds, the latter of which would not validate calibration.

[Reproducibility/presentation] The manuscript's code link is blank, and essential choices such as the main posterior sample count, complete epoch/batch-size schedules, random seeds, and sufficiently precise data/model construction details are missing. Reported efficiency tables exclude Laplace fitting and inference from the primary cost metric, so the end-to-end comparison is incomplete even if Figure 1c suggests modest overhead.

[Ethics/limitations] The impact statement says no societal consequences require discussion despite proposing a stronger privacy attack. A responsible treatment should address dual-use risks, authorization for auditing, and safeguards. The limitations discussion also does not acknowledge the central exchangeability/calibration issue. Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but the paper's principal theoretical and calibrated-testing claims are materially unsupported, preventing acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Using a post-hoc last-layer Laplace approximation to obtain many sample-specific MIA scores from one reference model is an interesting and potentially useful efficiency direction.
Empirical scope: The evaluation spans five image/tabular and five text datasets, multiple architectures, low-FPR operating points, and both architecture and distribution mismatch settings.

The reported empirical gains are substantial. For example, Table 1 reports 35.75% TPR at 1% FPR on CIFAR-100 using one reference model, versus 23.20% for eight-model LiRA, while requiring much less reference-model training.

The paper includes useful ablations over posterior sample count, curvature factorization, alternative approximate-Bayesian methods, and multi-reference scaling. The distinction between posterior uncertainty around one dataset and variation across reference datasets is also acknowledged in Appendix A.3.
Presentation is generally organized and readable, and the authors explicitly note Gaussian-approximation limitations and suggest held-out calibration when scores are non-Gaussian.
weaknesses: Soundness: The null model underlying Algorithm 1 is not justified. The target is a conventionally trained point estimate, whereas the reference scores are posterior samples conditional on one fixed reference dataset. The assertion that the target score has the same distribution and variance as those posterior scores does not follow. Indeed, Appendix A.3 observes that posterior samples fluctuate around a dataset-specific estimator while retrained estimators fluctuate across datasets. Treating these as exchangeable double-counts or conflates distinct uncertainty sources.

Algorithm 1 cannot estimate the inter-dataset variation caused by using only one reference dataset. Its sample variance measures posterior variation around that reference model, yet the target/reference discrepancy also contains the potentially substantial random offset between their training datasets. Consequently, the claimed Student-t null distribution and nominal p-values need not be calibrated. Empirical ROC thresholding may still yield a useful attack score, but it does not validate the stated hypothesis test.

Theorem 3.2 is false or at least materially incomplete as stated. It claims strict monotonic improvement for every alpha in (0,1), while the proof requires alpha<0.5, assumes positive intra-model variance and a continuous alternative, treats the random sample mean as fixed, and ignores the dependence of the t critical value and degrees of freedom on M. Thus it does not establish the advertised general guarantee.

The proof that conditional attacks always outperform marginal attacks (Proposition B.2) contains unjustified algebra and inequalities. Equation 32 effectively factors an expectation of a ratio/product into products of expectations without an independence assumption. Subsequent Jensen steps also depend on the sign of the numerator and can reverse in the low-TPR regime assumed by the proof. Variance decomposition alone does not imply the claimed universal TPR ordering.

Algorithm 2 subtracts the within-model contribution when estimating inter-model variance, so the estimate can be negative at finite K. No clipping, constrained estimator, or fallback is specified, even though a negative value can invalidate the reported standard deviation and Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

The uncertainty interpretation is overstated. Sampling last-layer weights principally represents approximate parameter uncertainty; it does not by itself demonstrate that both aleatoric and epistemic components of the conditional score distribution are captured. Conversely, the claim that quantile regression only captures aleatoric uncertainty conflates uncertainty in an estimated quantile with the conditional outcome distribution.

Evidence: Most headline low-FPR results appear to come from one target-model/data split. At 0.1% FPR, estimates can be controlled by very few false positives, but confidence intervals or repetitions over target training and data partitions are absent. Table 9 varies reference models only on CIFAR-10 and does not resolve target-level uncertainty. The Gaussian diagnostics show only four selected examples and therefore provide weak support for tail calibration across datasets.

The efficiency comparison reports reference-training GPU minutes rather than a consistently measured end-to-end cost including curvature construction, prior tuning, posterior inference, and all baseline tuning. This makes the strength of the efficiency claim difficult to verify, particularly because QMIA's hyperparameter-search cost is included while the accounting for BMIA tuning is unclear.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The displayed code link is empty, and important details such as epochs, batch sizes, learning-rate schedules, random seeds, exact posterior sample counts used in main tables, preprocessing, and uncertainty over repeated runs are missing.

Presentation/ethics: The manuscript is visually clear, but several claims use stronger language than the supporting theory permits. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting, which is insufficient for a method explicitly designed to strengthen privacy attacks; dual-use risks, responsible use, and relevant mitigations should be discussed. Overall, the empirical idea has merit, but unsupported central statistical and theoretical claims prevent acceptance in its present form.

strengths: The core idea—using a post-hoc last-layer Laplace approximation to obtain many conditional score samples from one reference model—is practically appealing and appears original in the membership-inference setting.

The empirical study is broad, covering image, tabular, and text datasets, several architectures, architecture and distribution mismatch, OOD queries, alternative Bayesian approximations, Hessian factorizations, and a multi-reference extension.
Reported attack performance is often substantially stronger than the included baselines, especially at low false-positive rates; the ablations generally support the usefulness of posterior sampling.

The manuscript is organized clearly and includes useful implementation and complexity discussions. It also acknowledges non-Gaussian-score calibration as a limitation and suggests held-out/conformal calibration.
Using only a last-layer structured curvature approximation makes the approach considerably more scalable than a full-network Laplace approximation.
weaknesses: The central statistical model is not justified. Proposition 3.1 assumes that the target-model score s0 has the same distribution as posterior score samples from a fixed reference model, assigning Var(s0)=sigma_inter^2+sigma_intra^2. In the stated experiment, however, the target and reference models are separately trained MAP models; s0 is not a posterior draw around the fixed reference model. The linear-regression discussion explicitly notes the dataset-specific center gap but does not repair this assumption.

Algorithm 1 is inconsistent with the paper's own variance decomposition. With K=1, Equation 12 contains 2 sigma_inter^2+(1+1/M)sigma_intra^2, whereas Algorithm 1 estimates only variability among posterior samples and uses sqrt(1+1/M) times that estimate. Thus the claimed Student-t null distribution and nominal false-positive control do not follow. Empirical ROC ranking may still work, but it does not validate the advertised calibrated hypothesis test.

Theorem 3.2 is not established. Its proof treats the sample mean and the t critical value/degrees of freedom as fixed while changing M, and infers a strict power increase merely from a non-decreasing CDF. These omitted dependencies and the lack of conditions for strictness invalidate the claimed monotonic guarantee.

Proposition B.2 contains invalid steps. Equation 32 factors an expectation involving correlated, instance-dependent means and variances without an independence assumption. Later Jensen steps also ignore that the relevant numerator is negative in the stated low-TPR regime, which reverses inequalities. Consequently, the claimed general proof that conditional attacks dominate marginal attacks is unsupported.

The multi-reference estimator can produce a negative estimate of sigma_inter^2 after subtracting sigma_intra^2/M, but no clipping, constrained estimator, or failure handling is specified; the subsequent square root and degrees-of-freedom calculation may then be undefined.

The efficiency comparison counts only reference-model training in the main tables, excluding Laplace fitting and inference. Figure 1 shows that this additional cost can be comparable to training a reference model, so statements such as one-eighth computational cost and 'minimal' overhead are not supported by an end-to-end comparison, particularly for ImageNet and text models.

Evidence at 0.1% FPR is statistically fragile: the paper does not report evaluation-set counts, confidence intervals, or repeated target-model runs. Table 9 varies only the reference model, and on smaller datasets 0.1% FPR may correspond to approximately one or very few false positives. This weakens the headline low-FPR comparisons.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The promised code URL is absent, the default posterior sample count is unclear, and important details such as epochs, batch sizes, seeds, exact splits, text fine-tuning settings, and complete Laplace-optimization settings are missing.
The limitations discussion addresses Gaussianity but not the more fundamental target-versus-reference distribution mismatch, the unverified t-test calibration, or low-FPR sampling uncertainty.

The impact statement is boilerplate and claims no specific societal consequences despite presenting a stronger privacy attack. A meaningful dual-use discussion, responsible-release considerations, and possible mitigations are warranted. Overall, the promising empirical heuristic does not compensate for unsupported central theoretical and calibration claims.
